idiom_name: Ktor route handler + Exposed transaction { } (or Spring Boot @Transactional)
implementation_notes: Kotlin's script is a route handler or a repository/service method, and the transaction boundary comes from the framework rather than from the script. With Exposed every DSL/DAO operation must run inside transaction { }, which commits when the block returns and rolls back when it throws; suspendTransaction (or withContext(Dispatchers.IO)) is the non-blocking form, and the official Ktor+Exposed tutorial wraps it in a small withTransaction helper. On Spring Boot the equivalent is @Transactional on a @Service method. Either way the hand-written commit/rollback pair disappears; an explicit transaction block is still used when a script touches several data sources or needs a non-default isolation level.
pitfalls: Exposed's transaction() is blocking and runs on the calling thread: calling it directly in a coroutine blocks the dispatcher instead of suspending.
Nested transaction { } blocks are not independent transactions by default - check the nesting semantics before relying on partial rollback.
Catching the exception inside the transaction block and returning normally commits the partial work; let it propagate or mark the transaction rollback-only.
